item.title: Improved Parameterization of Snow Albedo in WRF/Noah-MP: Methodology Based on Snow Ablation in Upper Yellow River
item.dc:creator: Zongzhen Bian, Shihao Chen, Lu Xiang, Baohui Men, Hongrui Wang
item.description:
Journal of Climate — matched: surface energy balance, albedo, parameterization
Abstract Snow ablation processes have been shown to exert a significant influence on the management of water resources, as well as on the prevention of drought and flood within basin. However, modeling these processes remains challenging due to complex physics and topography. This study develops an improved snow albedo (ISA) scheme for the Noah-MP land surface model that dynamically integrates snow age, depth, and temperature to refine the albedo decay process. We implemented this scheme in WRF model to simulate a severe snow accumulation and ablation event in the Upper Yellow River basin from January to March 2008. Compared to the default Noah-MP (CLASS/BATS) schemes, our improved scheme significantly enhances simulation accuracy. It reduces the mean bias for snow cover fraction (SCF) to 4.19% (from >20%), decreases the surface albedo RMSE by at least 34% (to 0.069), and substantially mitigates the air temperature cold bias, cutting its RMSE by approximately 33.6% (1.1°C). The results demonstrate that a more physical representation of snow albedo is key to improving the surface energy balance and reducing the pervasive cold bias in regional climate simulations over complex terrain. This work provides a validated and effective approach for enhancing snow process modeling in high-altitude regions.

item.title: Evaluation of turbulent flux parameterizations over a continental glacier on the Tibetan Plateau
item.dc:creator: Yichan Xu, Meilin Zhu, Jing Gao, Daijiao Lin, Lei Hui, Fei Zhu, … (+2)
item.description:
The Cryosphere — matched: glacier, parameterization, heat wave
Glaciers on the Tibetan Plateau are losing mass, yet their turbulent heat exchange with the atmosphere remains uncertain. Using direct observations from the Dunde Glacier (May–October 2023), we analyzed turbulent flux variations at the glacier surface and evaluated five turbulent flux methods. We also showed that during a humid heatwave, turbulent heat input rose sharply and accelerated melt, highlighting the need to improve models under extreme conditions.

item.title: Retrieving Tropical Cyclone Intensity from Climate Reanalysis using Deep Learning
item.dc:creator: Minh-Khanh Luong, Chanh Kieu
item.description:
Journal of Climate — matched: reanalysis, neural network, downscaling
Abstract Traditional methods for improving tropical cyclone (TC) intensity from climate model outputs or projections have primarily relied on either dynamical or statistical downscaling. With recent advances in deep learning (DL) techniques, it is of interest to examine how DL can provide an alternative approach for enhancing TC intensity and structure retrieval from climate data. Using a common DL architecture based on convolutional neural networks (CNN) and a set of key environmental features relevant to TCs, we show that TC intensity and size can be effectively retrieved from climate reanalysis data without requiring super-resolution enhancement as in previous studies, even when applied to coarse-resolution climate data. This approach allows for retrieving TC intensity metrics and size that are dynamically constrained by the data, rather than estimating these quantities independently. Our results highlight that TC intensity and size are governed not only by TC internal processes but also by local environments during TC development for which DL models can learn and capture. The performance of our DL model depends on several factors such as season, the stage of TC development, or ocean basins, with root-mean-square errors ranging from ≈8–10 ms −1 for the maximum 10-m wind, ≈10–13 hPa for minimum central pressure, and ≈13–21 km for the radius of the maximum wind. Although these errors are better than any direct vortex detection or statistical downscaling methods applied to the same data, their wide ranges also suggest that a 0.5°-resolution climate data may contain limited TC information for DL models to learn from, regardless of model optimizations or architectures. Possible improvements and challenges in addressing the lack of fine-scale TC information in coarse-resolution climate reanalysis datasets are discussed.

item.title: TORRENT: An observation-constrained and benchmark-ready community shared dataset in the contiguous United States for flash-flood research and model intercomparison
item.dc:creator: Songkun Yan, Mengye Chen, Jonathan J. Gourley, Jian Zhang, Günter Blöschl, Paul Bates, … (+9)
item.description:
Earth System Science Data — matched: model intercomparison
Preprint under review for ESSD (discussion: open, 0 comments) Flash floods develop quickly, but the records needed to study them are scattered across many sources. We created TORRENT by linking flood reports, rainfall, river flow, drainage-area information, and field measurements across the contiguous United States. It contains 42 466 reported events and 806 ready-to-use case packages, including 21 carefully checked cases. Its open, machine-readable design will help people and artificial intelligence tools study floods and compare prediction methods.

item.title: Variable Masking for Climate Emulation in ACE
item.dc:creator: Alexey Yermakov, Troy Arcomano, Jeremy McGibbon, Brian Henn, Oliver Watt-Meyer
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: model intercomparison, emulator
arXiv:2610.21012v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the recent AI Model Intercomparison Project (AIMIP) benchmark, the ACE2.1-ERA5 emulator was shown to underestimate the true near-surface warming trend both during the training period and the out-of-sample extrapolation period. In this work, we present M-ACE2S (Masked-ACE2S), a modified version of the stochastic ACE2S model, which uses variable masking during training and reduces the reliance of M-ACE2S on any single input channel. We show that M-ACE2S improves long-term near-surface air temperature prediction. We also present a novel data normalization strategy called "global mean removal", which, combined with masking, further improves the near-surface temperature forecasts. We show that M-ACE2S outperforms the ACE2S baseline on in-sample data for ERA5 while improving training stability and generalizability of near-surface temperature to unseen forcing when paired with global mean removal.

item.title: Causal Fingerprints Reveal Hidden Mechanisms in Partially-Observed Dynamical Systems
item.dc:creator: Zhang Jiang, Marios Andreou, Nan Chen
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: dynamical system
arXiv:2610.22286v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In partially-observed dynamical systems, distinct hidden mechanisms can produce similar observable summary statistics while explaining individual events differently. We introduce causal fingerprints: realization-dependent patterns that track how information about a hidden state is revealed through subsequent evolution. Within a prescribed dynamical model, we compare the filtering posterior, based on observations up to a given time, with the smoothing posterior, obtained after adding an expanding window of future observations. We quantify this retrospective information gain using Kullback-Leibler divergence and track its evolution as the future window of observational data expands. The fingerprint reveals both the strength and temporal reach of hidden influence, which can vary across events and their stages. Because the observed trajectory is held fixed while hidden-state inference depends on the candidate model, fingerprints reveal how competing dynamical mechanisms explain the same observations even when selected statistics agree. In linear Gaussian systems, we derive a characteristic fingerprint timescale for the temporal reach of hidden influence. Calibrated surrogates matching the observable mean, variance, and decorrelation time can still produce distinct fingerprints when feedback memory, hidden-noise memory, or hidden forcing timescales are misrepresented. Nonlinear examples reveal mechanism-dependent signatures for extreme bursts, oscillatory variability, and regime switching, including multiplicative instability versus additive forcing, deterministic nonlinear feedback versus state-dependent multiplicative noise, and intrinsic bistability versus hidden double-well forcing. Causal fingerprints therefore provide a time- and event-resolved diagnostic for asking not only whether a model reproduces observed statistics, but how its hidden dynamics explain individual events.

item.title: Brief communication: Mass balance of glaciers in the Eastern Hindu Kush from 1979 to 2002 using KH-9 panoramic and SPOT-5 stereo imagery
item.dc:creator: Azka Ramzan, Sajid Ghuffar
item.description:
The Cryosphere — matched: glacier, mass loss
In the Hindu Kush region, there is a scarcity of observations on the mass balance of glaciers during the pre-2000 period. Here, using stereo imagery from satellites, we estimate that glaciers in the Eastern Hindu Kush have undergone mass loss at a moderate rate during 1979–2002. This study analyzes the behavior of debris-covered and debris-free glaciers as well as surging and non-surging glaciers. We further discuss individual glaciers and identify the major retreating glaciers in the region.

item.title: TailWeather: from tail to extremes, a global climatological dataset for machine-learning weather forecasting
item.dc:creator: Zhi-Song Liu, Michael Boy, Risto Makkonen
item.description:
Earth System Science Data — matched: machine learning, heat wave
Preprint under review for ESSD (discussion: open, 0 comments) Weather forecasts are mostly judged on ordinary days, not on the rare heatwaves, cold spells, storms, downpours, and droughts that cause most harm. We built a global daily record of such unusual weather over land since 1981 and compared it with reported disasters. Rarer weather was more often linked to harm, but disaster records miss much of the world. Leading artificial intelligence forecasts often missed extremes, especially strong winds, so forecasts need testing on extremes everywhere.

item.title: NUKLEUS—A First Convection-Permitting Multimodel Ensemble for Germany: Assessment of Future Changes in Temperature and Precipitation Extremes
item.dc:creator: Christian Beier, Katrin Ziegler, Heiko Paeth, Joaquim Ginete Pinto, Kevin Sieck, Lars Buntemeyer, … (+8)
item.description:
Journal of Climate — matched: ensemble, climate change, global warming
Abstract This study analyzes a novel nine-member ensemble of convection-permitting regional climate simulations for Germany to assess projected changes in temperature and precipitation extremes under two future global warming levels, +2 and +3 K. The robustness of the climate change signals within the ensemble is also evaluated to ensure the reliability of the results. Throughout the twenty-first century, temperature-related extremes are projected to intensify, with nighttime extremes showing larger increases than daytime extremes. This amplification of nocturnal warming implies elevated risks to human health and ecosystems. While annual precipitation sums in Germany are projected to change only slightly and are mostly not statistically significant, the frequency and intensity of intense and very extreme precipitation events increase substantially. This change signal is particularly evident in summer, despite a predominantly decreasing seasonal mean rainfall. Such contrasting changes indicate a future characterized by generally drier summers interrupted by heavy rainfall events, with implications for both droughts occurrence and flood risk estimates. Temperature-related extremes show high robustness across almost all of Germany, whereas precipitation-related extremes exhibit greater variability, reflecting stronger natural variability and model uncertainty. The high-resolution simulations reveal added value for temperature-based indices, including more detailed spatial patterns of time averages and changes in specific areas, together with reduced uncertainty as indicated by ensemble spread and signal-to-noise ratios. These new climate model projections offer a robust scientific basis and a high potential for developing adaptation strategies tailored to small-scale landscape units.

item.title: KNOU-Flood: Advancing global streamflow forecasting with lead-aware probabilistic machine learning
item.dc:creator: Minjong Cheon
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: reanalysis, ensemble, machine learning
arXiv:2610.20640v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Global streamflow forecasting supports flood preparedness, yet data-driven models trained on reanalysis lose skill when driven by operational forecasts, increasingly so with lead time. AIFL addresses this shift with a two-stage transfer-learning recipe and a deterministic LSTM, but it feeds one forecast lead time into the whole input window and gives no uncertainty. We ask how far this open recipe can be extended without changing its recurrent core. KNOU-Flood keeps a single-layer LSTM and the two-stage training and changes the information around it: a longer input window (424 days), lead-aware forecast inputs, GraphCast as a second forecast source next to ECMWF HRES, and a latent-noise ensemble trained with the fair CRPS. We compare against a re-implementation of the AIFL recipe (its code is not public) under identical data, stations, splits and metrics. Our contributions are threefold. First, over three seeds and 2,099 test basins (2021-2023), KNOU-Flood reaches a median KGE' of 0.65 at LT1 and 0.48 at LT10 against 0.62 and 0.34, with significant gains at all ten lead times under two scoring protocols, also against a 1024-unit baseline and on held-out basins (one seed each). Second, identical weights give an LT10 KGE' of 0.18 or 0.34 depending on how forecasts are fed, so much of the lead-time decay reported for AIFL is an input-protocol effect; the probabilistic head contributes most to the gain, followed by the raw GraphCast channels, the longer window and mixed fine-tuning. Third, the ensembles reach lower CRPS than probabilistic versions of the baseline, are nearly calibrated with inference-time dropout, and detect 1.5- and 2-year floods better than all baselines; the benefit for rarer floods depends on the seed, and an exploratory tail-weighted variant improves 10-year and larger events. KNOU-Flood is a controlled extension of an open recipe, not a new architecture.

item.title: On the theoretical limitations of joint inversion for basal slipperiness and effective viscosity in ice-flow models
item.dc:creator: Camilla A. O. Schelpe, G. Hilmar Gudmundsson
item.description:
The Cryosphere — matched: ice sheet
In this study, we investigate the ability to extract information about ice viscosity at the same as basal slipperiness in the inversion procedure of large-scale ice-sheet models. This is an essential part of the initialisation of many large-scale computational ice-sheet models. However, there is a lack of consensus on whether a joint inversion is possible to determine these fields. We present a theoretical framework to better understand the factors influencing the retrieval.

item.title: Can AI Forecast the Extremes? Evaluating Probabilistic Weather Models on Tropical Cyclones
item.dc:creator: Nathan Chalumeau, Xavier Renard, Remi Meynadier, Hugo Rakotoarimanga, Marcin Detyniecki, Emmanuel de Bezenac
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: ensemble, extreme event
arXiv:2610.22077v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Weather prediction is undergoing an important shift, with data-driven AI models outperforming leading numerical weather prediction systems on average at a fraction of the computational cost. Yet, whether this success extends to extreme events remains contested. Earlier evaluations have exposed important shortcomings, but have largely focused on deterministic models and metrics, leaving the capabilities of the latest probabilistic models less understood. We conduct an extensive benchmark of tropical cyclone forecasting, comparing GenCast, FourCastNet 3, and FGN with ECMWF's operational physics-based ensemble, IFS-ENS. We develop a suite of probabilistic metrics and diagnostic analyses to assess cyclone tracking, intensity biases, uncertainty, and the wind-pressure relationship that characterizes storm structure. We find that, despite remaining limitations in intensity and ensemble spread, leading AI models substantially outperform IFS-ENS in cyclone tracking: FGN achieves better probabilistic location scores for 90% of evaluated storms in 2025. Further analyses reveal model-specific failure modes and suggest a lingering influence of pretraining data, pointing to opportunities for targeted improvement. Nonetheless, these results suggest that AI models are capable of capturing physical relationships that remain predictive well beyond typical weather conditions, motivating further investigation into how these capabilities emerge and how to strengthen them.

item.title: Meso-NH-ISO v1.0: a water stable isotopologue scheme in the non-hydrostatic mesoscale atmospheric model Meso-NH – application to a 2D West African squall line
item.dc:creator: Christelle Barthe, Françoise Vimeux, Camille Risi, Sören François
item.description:
Geoscientific Model Development
We implemented water stable isotopologues in the non-hydrostatic mesoscale atmospheric model Meso-NH. We validated this isotopic version (Meso-NH-ISO) with a simulation of a well-documented squall line in the Sahel region. In future works, simulations with Meso-NH-ISO will be done on real cases of cyclones or squall lines. The goal is to better interpret and quantify isotopic observations on the field in terms of atmospheric processes that drive development and intensity of those thunderstorms.
